name: Executive order of November 9, 1871 approving the Tularosa River (Tularosa Valley) reservation for the Southern Apache
nations: Fort Sill Apache Tribe (Chihenne or Warm Springs Apache, and Chiricahua Apache)
promises: This was an executive order, not a treaty. Royce's schedule records that the President approved the selection of a reserve known as the Tularosa River reservation, running from the headwaters of the Tularosa River and its tributaries downstream ten miles on each side for thirty miles.
No cession was made and no payment was offered for the Warm Springs and Chiricahua homeland around it.
landTaken: Royce area 531, the Tularosa River reservation. The Commission's boundary for the Chiricahua lands taken in 1886 runs northward along the Tularosa River from its meeting with the San Francisco River (Finding 13(a)). No acreage for the reservation was found in a source opened.
compensation: None at the time. The Commission valued the Chiricahua tract of Dockets 30-A and 48-A at $15,975,000 (June 9, 1971); the final judgment of August 25, 1971 awarded $15,967,300 in those dockets, after a stipulated offset of $7,700, and $521,796 in Dockets 30 and 48 for the adjoining tract.
today: In Dockets 30-A and 48-A the Indian Claims Commission found that no treaty or agreement of cession ever became operative with the Chiricahua Apache, including the Warm Springs band, that their lands 'were taken by the United States without consent or compensation of the Indians' (Finding 11), and that reservations were established for them within their territory in 1871 to 1875 before the Government moved them to San Carlos from 1876 (Finding 6(h)). It dated the taking of their aboriginal title to September 4, 1886, the surrender of Geronimo (Finding 14), and its findings do not mention the Tularosa reservation or its revocation. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe, descendants of the Chiricahua and Warm Springs Apache, holds a reservation at Akela, New Mexico, within its historic territory; its history page says the reservation proclamation was issued in November 2011.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: a presidential order approving the Tularosa River reservation in New Mexico, ten miles on each side of the river for thirty miles. No cession was made and no payment was offered for the homeland around it.
plain.happened: No finding of a breach of this order was found. The Indian Claims Commission found in 1968 that Chiricahua lands, including the Warm Springs band's, were taken without consent or compensation, but it dated that taking to 1886.
plain.today: In 1971 the Commission awarded $15,967,300 and $521,796 for Chiricahua lands; whether these were paid has not been traced. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe says its reservation at Akela, New Mexico was proclaimed in November 2011.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its ancestors lived in southwestern New Mexico, southeastern Arizona and northern Mexico until they were forcibly removed and held as prisoners of war by the United States from 1886 to 1914.

openQuestions: The order's own text was not opened; the UGA copy linked in treaties.json (531r.pdf) did not load on 2026-11-08. Royce dates it November 9, 1871, but Royce's later entry for the restoration refers to an order of August 29, 1871 (OCR), and a digitized compilation of executive orders cross-references an order of November 7, 1871. The exact date is unsettled.

Whether the whole reservation lay inside the Commission's Chiricahua tract was not plotted: the tract boundary follows the Tularosa River, so the reservation straddled it, and the Commission's 1970 award in Dockets 30 and 48 covered a further tract to the north.

treaties.json lists all seven federally recognized Apache tribes; Royce's 'Apache (Southern)' are the Warm Springs and related Chiricahua bands, represented today by the Fort Sill Apache Tribe (some descendants also live on the Mescalero reservation). Treaties.json was not edited.
The Fort Sill Apache history page says a land claim was settled in the mid-1970s; the Commission's records show the value was decided by the Commission and only the offsets were stipulated.

Audit 2026-11-08: status lowered from broken to no-breach-found. The only breach was the Commission's Chiricahua finding in Dockets 30-A and 48-A, which dates the taking of aboriginal title to September 4, 1886 and does not name the Tularosa reservation, its creation or its 1874 revocation; it is not a finding that this order was broken. The finding is kept in 'today' as context. Decided by Jordan 2026-11-08: an executive order taking back executive-order land is not a breach by itself; it needs a finding. Plain lines updated to match.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for: Court of Claims names "apache" (Fort Sill Apache appeals of 1973-1979 concern Dockets 30 and 30-A, already weighed in the audit); ICC full text "Tularosa". Nothing new.
